title: Designing a Home for a Three-Generation Family: Private Yet Connected
desc: Design ideas for a three-generation home: grandparents' room on a low floor, shared space, the young couple's private area, safe bathrooms, elevator planning.
summary: Layout principles for a home where grandparents, parents and children live together: zoning by generation, shared space, safety for seniors and the ability to change over time.
body: p

Many Vietnamese families still live three generations under one roof. Grandparents need quiet and safe movement; the young couple needs privacy; young children need space to play and study. A good design gives each generation its own space while the whole family stays connected. Below are the main principles.
h2
1. Grandparents' room: prioritize the ground floor or the second floor
ul
Put the grandparents' bedroom on the lowest floor possible, near the kitchen and shared living room so they do not have to climb stairs many times a day.
The room should have an en-suite bathroom adjoining it, a wide door, and no level difference between the bedroom and bathroom.
Provide a window to catch morning sun, with good ventilation; avoid placing it next to the parking area or the noisy street side.
In a townhouse, if the ground floor is used for parking or business, put the grandparents' room on the second floor with a staircase that has landings and handrails on both sides.
h2
2. Shared space is the “heart” of the home
p

The living room, kitchen and dining area should be connected or close together and spacious, so the whole family can eat and chat together. This is also where the grandparents watch the grandchildren while the parents cook. If possible, add a small shared living room on an upper floor as a study and movie corner for the children.
h2
3. Private area for the young couple and children
ul
Put the young couple's bedroom on a different floor, or at a different end of the house from the grandparents' room, to reduce noise and keep privacy.
Place the children's room near the parents' room while the children are small; design a room that can be split in two or merged when the children grow up.
A larger house can add a secondary kitchen and a separate entrance for each small family.
h2
4. Safety for seniors and young children
ol
Non-slip floors in bathrooms, the kitchen and balconies; limit level differences inside the house.
Grab bars in the bathroom, beside the toilet and in the shower area.
Bright enough lighting on walkways and stairs; easy-to-reach switches, with night lights.
Sturdy balcony railings, light wells and stairs, with small gaps.
Electrical outlets in positions safe for young children; in the kitchen, cabinets holding knives and chemicals can be locked.
p
For details on safe staircases, see our separate article on staircase position and style in the home.
h2
5. Design to change over time
p
Families change: children grow and need their own rooms, and grandparents become frailer and need more help. It is advisable to:
ul
Plan an elevator shaft in the structure for a house of 4 floors or more, even if it is not installed right away.
Use light partitions in some rooms so space is easy to divide or merge.
Run spare electrical and water conduits in advance for a bathroom or secondary kitchen on an upper floor.
p
Adding floors or changing the structure later may require an adjustment of the permit and an engineer to check load-bearing capacity. See Adjusting and extending a construction permit.
h2
6. Notes on floor area and legal matters
ul

A three-generation home usually has a large floor area. A house of 3 floors or more, or with a floor area of 250 m² or more, must be designed by a qualified organization or individual (Clause 2, Article 10 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP).
If you want to separate part of the house and land for a child later, find out the conditions for subdividing the land plot from the start so that access and structure can be arranged accordingly.
p

note

This article is for reference; each building needs a survey and design by a qualified person. Structural solutions for an elevator shaft, adding floors or changing use must be calculated by an engineer according to the existing condition of the building.
